newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa in longest upswing ever - Boland.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa in longest upswing ever - Boland.

text.p: South Africa is far from entering a recession and is still in the longest upswing period in its recent history, Boland Bank economist Francois Jansen said on Wednesday.

"Although certain observers have difficulty in believing it, the fact is that the average economic growth rate over the past four years was roughly 2.6 percent," Jansen said in his latest Economic Review report.
He said the current upswing period had been in place for 16 consecutive quarters compared to the average length of upswings since the Second World War of 8.8 quarters.
It was still firmly established and it was difficult to see what could plunge the economy into recession between now and at least the year 2000.
The optimism was based on the fact that the upswing was based on sound financial principles and had not been "bought" through low interest rates, Jansen said.
He expected the prime overdraft rate to be cut in September or October with two further cuts in 1998.
"The lower interest rates will provide welcome relief which will in turn favour private consumer spending," Jansen said.

The benefits of last year's exchange rate depreciation were now reflected in the export market and exporters would have about 12 months to enjoy these benefits before higher inflation kicked in again.

The further liberalisation of foreign exchange controls would improve South Africa's rating in international markets, attracting foreign inflows directed at investments rather than portfolios, Jansen said.
